questions.statement: Complete the sentence: "She _____ (visit) Cartagena three times."
questions.context: A teacher in Bogotá asks students about the present perfect tense.

options.feedback: Incorrect. This is the base form.
Correct. Present perfect: has + past participle.

questions.explanation:
El present perfect se forma con have/has + past participle. Se usa para acciones que ocurrieron en un tiempo no especificado del pasado pero que tienen relevancia en el presente. "She has visited Cartagena three times" = tiene esa experiencia.

---

questions.statement: Which modal verb expresses obligation (something you have to do)?
questions.context: In Medellín, a student learns about modal verbs.
questions.explanation:
"Must" se usa para expresar obligación fuerte (must = deber/haber que). Ej: "You must study for the exam." Otra forma de expresar obligación es "have to". "Should" expresa recomendación, no obligación.

---

questions.statement: What is the meaning of "boarding pass"?
questions.context: In a language class in Cali, students read travel vocabulary.

options.text: A document to enter the country.
options.feedback: Incorrect. That's a passport or visa.

options.text: A ticket to buy at the airport.
options.feedback: Incorrect. You get it after check-in.

options.text: A document that allows you to board the plane.
options.feedback: Correct. You receive it after checking in.

questions.explanation:
El "boarding pass" (tarjeta de embarque) es el documento que se recibe después del check-in y permite abordar el avión. Contiene información como puerta de embarque (gate), asiento (seat) y hora de embarque (boarding time).

---

questions.context: In Barranquilla, a student learns when to use "should".

options.text: You must stop at the red light.

questions.explanation:
"Should" se usa para dar consejos o recomendaciones. Es menos fuerte que "must". "You should drink more water" = es recomendable, pero no obligatorio. La estructura es: subject + should + base verb.

---

questions.context: In Bucaramanga, a student writes about travel experiences.

options.text: I have go to Santa Marta.
I has gone to Santa Marta.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Has" is for third person singular (he/she/it).

options.text: I have gone to Santa Marta.
options.feedback: Correct. "I have gone" is the correct present perfect form.

options.text: I have went to Santa Marta.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Went" is simple past, not past participle.

questions.explanation:
El past participle de "go" es "gone" (no "went"). Recordar: go-went-gone. Con "have" (I/you/we/they) y "has" (he/she/it). "I have gone to Santa Marta" significa que tengo la experiencia de haber ido.

---

questions.statement: What do you call the place where you collect your bags after a flight?
questions.context: At the airport in Cartagena, a tourist needs vocabulary.

options.feedback: Incorrect. That's where you drop your bags.
Correct. Baggage claim is where you collect your luggage.
Incorrect. That's where they check your documents.

questions.explanation:
Vocabulario de viaje clave: baggage claim = reclamo de equipaje, check-in counter = mostrador de facturación, gate = puerta de embarque, security check = control de seguridad, carry-on = equipaje de mano.

---

questions.statement: Which sentence is in present perfect?
questions.context: A teacher explains the difference between simple past and present perfect.

options.feedback: Incorrect. This is simple past (specific time: last year).
Correct. Present perfect, no specific time.

questions.explanation:
El present perfect se usa cuando el tiempo NO es específico (I have visited Bogotá). El simple past se usa cuando el tiempo SÍ es específico (I visited Bogotá last year). Esta diferencia es fundamental para elegir el tiempo correcto.

---

questions.statement: Choose the correct modal verb: "Students _____ bring their ID to the trip."
questions.context: A student in Pereira writes rules for a school trip.

options.feedback: Correct. "Must" would be stronger. "Should" is appropriate for a recommendation. Actually, "must" is more accurate here.
Correct. "Must" expresses obligation, which fits school rules.

questions.explanation:
En reglas escolares, "must" expresa obligación: "must bring" = debe traer. "Should" sería más suave (recomendación). "Must not / mustn't" expresa prohibición: "mustn't run" = no debe correr.

---

questions.statement: What is the difference in meaning between these two sentences?
questions.context: A student compares two sentences: "You must study" and "You should study."

options.text: They mean exactly the same thing.
"Must" expresses obligation (it's required); "should" expresses advice (it's recommended but not required).

options.feedback: Incorrect. Both can be formal or informal.

questions.explanation:
"Must" = obligación (es necesario/requerido). "Should" = recomendación (es aconsejable pero no obligatorio). Ej: "You must take this medicine" (orden médica). "You should exercise" (recomendación de salud).

---

questions.context: A student in Cartagena writes a postcard using present perfect.

options.text: We have visited the Castillo de San Felipe yesterday.
We have visited the Castillo de San Felipe. It was amazing!
options.feedback: Correct. Present perfect without specific time.

options.text: We have visit the Castillo de San Felipe.
We has visited the Castillo de San Felipe.

questions.explanation:
Present perfect no se usa con expresiones de tiempo específico como "yesterday" (ayer), "last week" (la semana pasada), "in 2023". Con esas expresiones se usa simple past. Present perfect se usa con "ever", "never", "already", "yet", "just".

---

questions.context: A student says: "I have visited the Gold Museum last weekend."

options.feedback: Incorrect. It has a tense error.

options.text: No, it should be: "I visited the Gold Museum last weekend." Since "last weekend" is a specific time, we use simple past, not present perfect.
options.feedback: Correct. Present perfect doesn't combine with specific time expressions.

options.text: No, it should be: "I have visit the Gold Museum."
Yes, because present perfect can be used with any time expression.
options.feedback: Incorrect. It cannot be used with specific times.

questions.explanation:
Error común: usar present perfect con tiempo específico. "Last weekend" es específico → simple past. Present perfect requiere tiempo no especificado. Corrección: "I visited the Gold Museum last weekend."

---

questions.statement: Which sentence gives the BEST advice?
questions.context: A student wants to give travel advice to a friend going to Medellín.

options.feedback: Correct. Both "must" and "should" can work, but this expresses a strong recommendation.

options.text: You should visit the Comuna 13 graffiti tour.
options.feedback: Correct. "Should" gives specific advice. Both A and C could work, but C is more specific and natural.

questions.explanation:
Para dar consejos de viaje, "should" es el modal más apropiado. "You should visit..." expresa recomendación. "Must" también funciona para recomendaciones fuertes. "Can" (poder) no es consejo; "might" (quizás) expresa duda.

---

questions.statement: What is the difference in meaning between these two sentences?
questions.context: A student reads: "I have worked here for five years." vs. "I worked here for five years."

options.text: They mean exactly the same thing.
The first one means the job is definitely over.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Present perfect implies connection to present.

options.text: The first sentence (present perfect) implies the person still works there; the second (simple past) implies the job is finished.
options.feedback: Correct. Present perfect connects past action to present.

options.text: The first sentence is grammatically incorrect.

questions.explanation:
"I have worked here for five years" → sigo trabajando aquí. "I worked here for five years" → trabajé allí pero ya no. Present perfect conecta el pasado con el presente. Simple past indica acción terminada.

---

questions.context: A student says: "I must to study for the English exam."

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Must" is followed by base verb without "to."

options.text: No, it should be: "I must studied."
No, it should be: "I must study for the English exam." Modal verbs are followed by base form without "to."
options.feedback: Correct. After must/can/should, use base verb.

options.text: Yes, because "to" is necessary after all verbs.

questions.explanation:
Los verbos modales (must, can, should, may, might, will, would) siempre van seguidos del verbo en forma base sin "to". Error común: "must to go" → correcto: "must go". Ej: "She must study" (no "must to study").

---

questions.statement: Why does the teacher use both "must" and "should" in this sentence?
questions.context: A teacher says: "To communicate effectively in English while traveling, you must know key vocabulary, but you should also practice listening comprehension."

options.text: The teacher doesn't know the difference.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The teacher uses them correctly.

options.text: "Must" indicates essential knowledge (vocabulary), while "should" indicates advisable but less essential skill (listening practice).
options.feedback: Correct. The modals show different levels of importance.

options.text: Both words mean the same thing here.
"Should" is used because listening is more important.

questions.explanation:
La elección entre "must" y "should" comunica el nivel de importancia. "Must" (esencial/obligatorio) se usa para lo fundamental. "Should" (aconsejable/recomendable) se usa para lo complementario. Esta distinción permite matizar el mensaje.

questions.statement: Which of the following is a modal verb?
questions.context: A student in Bogotá is learning about modal verbs for the first time.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Play" is a main verb, not a modal verb.
Correct. "Must" is a modal verb used to express obligation or necessity.
Incorrect. "Walked" is a past simple verb.

questions.explanation:
Modal verbs (can, must, should, may, might, etc.) are auxiliary verbs that express necessity, possibility, permission, or ability. They are always followed by the base form of the main verb.

---

questions.statement: What is the correct structure after a modal verb?
questions.context: A teacher in Medellín asks about the structure of modal verbs.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Most modal verbs are NOT followed by "to" (except "ought to").

options.text: Modal verb + base form of the verb (infinitive without "to")
options.feedback: Correct. Example: "You must study" (not "must to study").
Incorrect. Modals are followed by the base form, not -ing.
Incorrect. That's for perfect modals or passive voice.

questions.explanation:
Modal verbs are followed by the base form of the verb (infinitive without "to"). The only exception is "ought to" which includes "to".

---

questions.statement: Choose the correct sentence to express that someone knows how to play the accordion:
questions.context: A student in Cali wants to express ability.

options.feedback: Correct. "Can" expresses ability (knowing how to do something).

questions.explanation:
"Can" is the modal verb used to express ability in the present. It means someone knows how to do something or is able to do it.

---

questions.statement: Which sentence expresses a strong obligation (necessity)?
questions.context: A student in Barranquilla needs to express obligation.

options.feedback: Correct. "Must" expresses a strong obligation or necessity.

options.text: You ought to arrive on time.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Ought to" expresses advice or mild obligation.

questions.explanation:
"Must" is used for strong obligation, often from the speaker's perspective. It is common in rules, laws, and strong personal necessities.

---

questions.statement: Which modal verb best completes this rule?
questions.context: Read the school rule: "Students _____ use their phones during class."

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Can" would mean it's allowed, which contradicts a school rule.
Incorrect. "Should" is advice, not a strong rule.

questions.explanation:
"Must not" (mustn't) is used to express prohibition - something that is not allowed. It is stronger than "shouldn't" which is just advice.

---

questions.statement: What does the tourist want to know?
questions.context: A tourist in Cartagena asks: "Where can I find a good restaurant?"

options.text: A recommendation for a must-visit place.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Can" here asks about possibility/ability, not obligation.

options.text: Information about the possibility of finding a restaurant.
options.feedback: Correct. "Can" in questions asks about possibility or availability.
Incorrect. "Can" here is about external possibility, not personal ability.

questions.explanation:
"Can" in questions can ask about possibility or availability. "Where can I find...?" means "Is it possible to find...?" or "Where is there...?"

---

questions.statement: Which modal verb best completes the doctor's advice?
questions.context: A doctor gives advice to a patient in Bogotá: "You _____ drink more water and exercise regularly."

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Must" is too strong for general health advice; "should" is more appropriate.
Correct. "Should" is used to give advice or recommendations.

questions.explanation:
"Should" is the modal verb used to give advice or make recommendations. It is less strong than "must" and more like a suggestion.

---

questions.statement: What is the meaning of "ought to" in this sentence?
questions.context: Read: "You ought to visit the Coffee Triangle when you go to Colombia."

options.text: It expresses a recommendation or strong advice.
options.feedback: Correct. "Ought to" is similar to "should" but slightly more formal.

questions.explanation:
"Ought to" is a semi-modal verb that means the same as "should" - it gives advice or expresses what is the right thing to do.

---

questions.statement: What type of modal meaning does "must" express here?
questions.context: A student sees a sign: "You must wear a mask inside the hospital."

options.feedback: Correct. "Must" in signs and rules expresses a requirement.

questions.explanation:
In public signs and official rules, "must" expresses a requirement or obligation. It is not optional - it's something you are required to do.

---

questions.statement: What does "may" express in this sentence?
questions.context: Read: "It may rain in the afternoon in Bogotá."

options.feedback: Incorrect. "May" does not express certainty, only possibility.
Correct. "May" expresses that something is possible but not certain.
Incorrect. Although "may" can express permission, here it expresses possibility.

questions.explanation:
"May" can express two things: possibility (it may rain = it's possible) and permission (you may go = you are allowed to go). Context determines the meaning.

---

questions.statement: What is the difference between "can" and "must" in these sentences?
questions.context: "You can use the library until 6 PM. You must be quiet inside."

options.feedback: Correct. "Can use" = allowed to use; "must be quiet" = required to be quiet.

questions.explanation:
"Can" often expresses permission in affirmative sentences (You can go = you are allowed). "Must" expresses obligation (something you have to do).

---

questions.statement: Which question is most polite to ask for permission?
questions.context: A student wants to ask for permission to leave the classroom in Bucaramanga.

options.feedback: Incorrect. This asks about obligation, not permission.
Most polite and formal. "May" is traditionally used to ask for permission.

questions.explanation:
"May I" is the most formal and polite way to ask for permission. "Can I" is also used in everyday English but is less formal.

---

questions.statement: What is the difference between "should" and "might" in B's response?
questions.context: Read the dialogue: A: "I have a headache." B: "You should take a rest. You might have the flu."

options.feedback: Correct. B recommends rest and suggests a possible cause.

questions.explanation:
"Should" is used for advice or recommendations (what you think is a good idea). "Might" is used for possibility (something that is possible but not certain).

---

questions.statement: Is this sentence logical? Why or why not?
questions.context: A student writes: "You mustn't study for the exam because it's easy."

options.text: Yes, it's logical. You don't need to study for an easy exam.
